title: Lawyer says scenario at jail cell 'a recipe for disaster'
article: Will Willier, the attorney for the family of Colleen Marie Akazay, called the scenario leading to her death in a cell "a recipe for disaster" on the final court day of her fatality inquiry Wednesday.

The 25-year-old was found dead while in the custody of the Grande Prairie RCMP at about 10:50 a.m. on Feb. 18, 2006 - just over seven hours after being arrested, along with her common-law husband Frank Ferguson, for public intoxication at Oasis Church.

Multiple bottles of prescribed medication and a baggy of powder were found in Akazay's possession at the time, and toxicology reports following her death revealed she died from a combination of alcohol, painkillers and sedatives in her system.
Testimony from her arresting officers, guards watching over her and the officer who found her dead all indicate her volatile situation was never recognized.

"It's a confluence of tragic circumstances ... some of the blame - if we are to assign blame - rests with Ms. Akazay, certainly, and some of the blame perhaps rests with members and guards at the RCMP detachment," said David Stam of the department of justice.

Tuesday's testimony reconstructed events at the time of Akazay's arrest and into the early hours of her morning in custody. On Wednesday, the focus shifted to what took placed after her body was discovered.

"She just seemed to be sleeping peacefully ... there were no signs of anything amiss in the cell," said Sgt. Ross Gear - supervising officer at the time - of his first impressions when coming on shift. That was shortly after his 6 a.m. start, said Gear.
When he returned to her cell around 10:50 a.m. - because Akazay was "next in line for release" - it was a different story.
"I opened the door and I called her name twice. There was no response, which I thought was a bit unusual. I moved forward and I believe I shook her.
"There was no response, and when I touched her hand and wrist they were cold," said Gear.
Akazay's lips were purple, with a "clear to whitish" fluid coming from them, according to Gear.
When he found no pulse, he shouted for assistance and a call to 911 was made.
With the help of other officers, he moved Akazay to the floor and waited for help.
He said he never did perform CPR, despite cell guard Pat Brignall's testimony Tuesday stating he had.
"In my mind, I believed she was gone at that point ... if I thought there was any chance that I could have done anything for her, I certainly would have," said Gear.

"There were police officers around, but not in the cell ... there was no CPR in progress at the time we had arrived," said Kerii Lee Albert, one of the attending Emergency Medical Services paramedics.
EMS workers cleared Azakay's airway and made brief attempts to resuscitate her, though it was quickly deemed too late to assist her. She was declared dead in her cell.

Raised again was the question of why the situation was not recognized for what it was as Akazay was booked, clearly intoxicated, holding a large quantity of prescription medication and then listed on booking forms as fumbling, falling, incoherent and angry.

Policy now, according to Gear, makes medical evaluation mandatory for any suspected combination of alcohol with narcotics or medication. At the time, however, that was not written, and largely came down to an officer's determination.
"I didn't suspect at that time that there was anything wrong with her ... she should have been sobered up or starting to sober up by that time," said Gear.
Const. Helen Pappas, Const. Matt Labelle and Const. Brandy Boychuk didn't suspect a problem would present itself either when they made the initial arrest at 3:15 a.m.
Gear admitted the signs were right there to be seen in the information provided on those booking forms, but said while officers do their best to look for them, on this occasion the signs were missed.

In addition to the changes in policy surrounding prisoners being fit for incarceration, the RCMP in Grande Prairie have also since moved to a newer, more modern facility, which allows constant prisoner monitoring through closed circuit television.
"Many (factors) this court could suggest be changed have been changed," said Stam.
Willier agreed, stating future focus should perhaps be on the level of officer training.

In particular, he noted the booking forms have not been significantly changed in light of policy updates. Items such as fumbling, falling, incoherent and angry are circled as they are noticed - if they are noticed - with no further instructions given.
"The (forms) have to marry up with these policies that they have now," said Willier.

Akazay's fatality inquiry is considered to be complete and pending any forthcoming written submissions or responses, there will be nothing further. Fatality inquiries are limited to establishing the cause, manner, time, place and circumstance of death, as well as the identity of the deceased.

Judge Jim Watson - who presided over this fatality inquiry - may make recommendations on the prevention of similar occurrences, but is prohibited from making findings of legal responsibility or assigning blame. Fatality inquiries are scheduled after all investigations into a matter are complete.

"This has been so hard ... I'm just glad this is over. She can rest in peace now. (But) it's good that they're doing something about it," said Akazay's mother, Rose Schamehorn, who observed the fatality inquiry alongside other family members.
